newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia must prepare for advent of EMU - bankers.
newsitem.headline: Croatia must prepare for advent of EMU - bankers.

text.p: Croatia sees a need to change its financial system to pave the way for the advent of the European Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999, the central bank governor Marko Skreb said on Tuesday.
"Forming of the EMU will have serious and long-term consequences on countries such as Croatia," Skreb told a seminar here organised by the central bank and Deutsche Bank.
"We must not forget that two thirds of our total foreign trade, both goods and services exports and imports, are with the European Union countries."

While a unified European export market with its single currency will reduce currency risks and hedging costs, it may toughen the battle among exporters from non-member countries and Croatia itself, Deutsche Bank's experts told reporters.
They said its commercial banks, particularly smaller ones, may soon find themselves pushed to the sidelines by a number of foreign competitors and investors seeking to buy them.

Skreb acknowledged the need for Croatian firms and banks to shape up and consolidate in order to face the competition but also pointed out stronger foreign investment as a positive outcome said Croatia can look forward to.
He said Croatia had already formed a working group charged with mulling possible effects of EMU and single currency on all segments of its economy, particularly the banking sector.
"Introduction of the Euro as a strong new currency...will probably change the world's financial currents, and Croatia is increasingly a part of them."
"We have to follow all the developments and examine their consequences so that we can adapt and be ready for them," the central bank head said, but he envisaged no major problems.
Most puzzling at this stage is how average citizens will react to the disappearance of the German mark -- a popular para-currency for household savings and property purchases.
"There may be some real psychological shocks when the mark ceases to exist as a legal tender in 2002," Skreb said.
Although Croatia is not likely to be among the first non-western transition economies to join the European Union, the EU membership and EMU are among its important long-term strategic goals, he said.

With the annual inflation projected at between 3 and 5 percent in the next three years and relatively low overall public debt, it already prides itself for meeting most of the Maastricht convergence criteria.
"Our interest rates are falling and we'll probably soon come up to standard in this as well," Skreb added.
